Law Name: Privacy Act 1988
Mapping Rationale: The Privacy Act 1988 is the primary federal legislation that governs protection of personal information and applies horizontally. The Act includes thirteen Privacy Principles, which set out standards, rights and obligations for the handling, holding, use, accessing and correction of personal information (including sensitive information. The Privacy Act's amendment in 2018 introduced a mandatory notification scheme for entities in responding to data breaches. The Notifiable Data Breach Scheme (NDB scheme) introduced an obligation to notify individuals whose personal information is involved in a data breach that is likely to result in serious harm. The NDB scheme applies to all agencies and organisations with existing personal information security obligations under the Australian Privacy Act. The Privacy Act's amendment in 2023 increases the maximum penalties for serious or repeated privacy breaches and provides the Australian Information Commissioner with greater powers to resolve privacy breaches and quickly share information about data breaches.
Notes: BGK Timeframe: Since December 1988, last amended in October 2024 | BGK Note: Since December 2022, the Privacy Act threatens higher penalties, namely the highest of AUD 50 million (approx. USD 33.1 million), three times the value of benefits obtained by the violation or 30% of local turnover. A current proposal aims to enable “action initiation” in the Consumer Data Right framework for sectoral data portability. In 2021, the Attorney General proposed an online privacy code for online platforms and data brokers, which did not advance to date.

Law Name: Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018
Mapping Rationale:
Australia's Cyber Security is guided through the 2023-2030 Australian Cyber Security Strategy, which includes a roadmap for new legislation and standards.

Until the new legislation under the strategy is passed, Cybersecurity is controlled through a mixture of laws including the Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018, Privacy Act 1988 and the Criminal Code Act 1995. These laws contain cybersecurity-related provisions dispersed across sectoral and thematic statutes, addressing critical infrastructure protection, data security, and cybercrime respectively, but they do not constitute a single, coherent, and horizontally applicable cybersecurity-specific legal framework.
Notes: BGK Timeframe: Since April 2018, last amended in October 2023 | BGK Note: Before parliament is a standalone Cyber Security Act to ensure strong laws and protections are in place through a clear legislative framework. The Legislative Package consists of the, Cyber Security Bill 2024, Intelligence Services and Other Legislation Amendment (Cyber Security) Bill 2024, Security of Critical Infrastructure and Other Legislation Amendment (Enhanced Response and Prevention) Bill 2024.

Law Name: Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act 1979
Mapping Rationale: The Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act 1979 requires a telecommunication service provider to keep specific telecommunications data relating to the services it offers for two years (187C). This retention scheme was inserted into the Act by the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Act 2015.
Notes: BGK Timeframe: Since October 1979, last amended in October 2024

Law Name: Privacy Impact Assessment 2020
Mapping Rationale: A Privacy Impact Assessment ('PIA') is contemplated by Australian privacy law but, apart from government agencies, is not mandated. However, arguably a PIA is, if not required, highly recommended to fulfil one's obligations under APP 1.2. The guidance and recommendations of the OAIC are that a PIA should be used for any new, changed/varied or altered process, method, or technology used that processes any personal information. In addition, the OAIC may, in writing, direct an agency to conduct a PIA, within a specified period if an agency proposes to engage in an activity or function involving the handling of personal information about individuals, and the OAIC considers that the activity or function might have a significant impact on the privacy of individual (Section 33D(1) of the Privacy Act).
Notes: BGK Timeframe: Since 2020

Law Name: Data Availability and Transparency Act 2022
Mapping Rationale: On 1 April 2022, the Data Availability and Transparency Act 2022 commenced, creating a new scheme for sharing Commonwealth Government data. Under the Act, authorised Commonwealth bodies can provide controlled access to public sector data to accredited users, being accredited state and federal government entities and public Australian universities, for specific purposes in the public interest. Specifically, under Article 104, if the Commissioner reasonably believes that a person has information or a document relevant to an investigation under section 101, or to any other of the Commissioner’s regulatory functions set out in section 45, the Commissioner may, by written notice given to the person, require the person to give the information, or produce the document, to the Commissioner within the period specified in the notice.
Notes: BGK Timeframe: Since March 2022, last amended October 2024

Law Name: Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act 1979
Mapping Rationale:
The Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act 1979 allows law enforcement to intercept user communications, even without a warrant in emergencies or for capability testing. It details various warrants like interception (Section 10) and stored communications (Section 110). Law Name: Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010
Mapping Rationale:
The Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010 (PDPA) prohibits the transfer of personal data out of Malaysia unless such transfer is to a country, which has been specified and recorded in the Official Gazette by the Minister. Currently, no countries have been specified officially. Notwithstanding the prohibition on transfers of personal data out of the country, the PDPA sets out a number of exceptions to the prohibition, such as where the consent of the data subject has been obtained for such transfer and where the transfer is necessary for the performance of a contract between the parties. When in doubt as to whether the exemptions on data transfer apply, the prudent approach would be to obtain consent from the data subject in respect of such out of Malaysia transfer. In relation to outsourcing, a data user is not allowed to share data with third parties unless the consent of the individual has been obtained.

The PDPA applies broadly across sectors to regulate the processing of personal data for commercial transactions. Any personal data processed in Malaysia must adhere to PDPA standards, including specific security and privacy principles. Section 6 requires that personal data should not be processed unless the data subject consents, or it is necessary for specific legal reasons. The Security Principle in Section 9 enforces practical steps to protect personal data from unauthorized or accidental access during processing, which aligns with local data storage requirements. Section 129 of the PDPA mentions restrictions on transferring personal data to places outside Malaysia unless the destination has data protection laws or the transfer meets specific conditions.

The Personal Data Protection Code of Practice for the Banking and Financial Sector 2017 mandates that personal data be processed according to PDPA principles. Specific rules about data transfer abroad are mentioned in the document, limiting cross-border data transfers without compliance. Similar requirements for the Communications Sector are set out in the Code of Practice for Licensees Under the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998, especially for network and service providers. Both banking and communications sectors mention compliance with the Data Transfer Abroad clause, ensuring that any cross-border data transfer adheres to Malaysia’s data protection standards duscussed in other relevant subpillars.
Notes:
BGK Timeframe: Since November 2013, last amended in 2024 | BGK Note: The 2024 amendments to Malaysia’s Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) introduce important changes aimed at strengthening data governance and aligning Malaysia’s privacy laws with international standards, such as the EU’s GDPR. A key feature of the amendments is the mandatory breach notification, requiring organizations to report data breaches to the Personal Data Protection Commissioner within 72 hours of detection. This is a significant shift towards greater transparency and accountability in data management.

In addition, the amendments expand the scope of responsibility to data processors, not just data controllers, holding both parties accountable for the protection and handling of personal data. Another critical update is the requirement for both controllers and processors to appoint Data Protection Officers (DPOs), reinforcing organizational responsibility for privacy practices.

The revisions also introduce stricter controls on cross-border data transfers, requiring organizations to conduct a thorough assessment of the receiving country’s data protection standards before transferring data internationally. This ensures that personal data sent abroad is subject to equivalent protections. The amendments significantly increase penalties for non-compliance, raising fines up to 1 million MYR and extending possible imprisonment terms to three years. The Personal Data Protection Commissioner is also granted broader powers to conduct proactive audits to ensure compliance.

Additionally, biometric data is now classified as sensitive personal data, warranting additional safeguards. These changes position Malaysia as a more attractive destination for foreign businesses, particularly in industries that handle significant volumes of data, such as data centers and digital operations

Law Name: Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010
Mapping Rationale:
Malaysia currently does not have a strict data localization law that mandates all personal data to be stored exclusively within the country. However, the Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010 includes provisions that regulate cross-border data transfers, requiring that personal data can only be transferred out of Malaysia if the recipient country provides an adequate level of data protection. This means that while data can be stored and processed abroad, certain safeguards must be in place to protect personal data.

For certain sectors, like banking and finance, there are sector-specific guidelines (e.g., the Banking and Financial Sector Code of Practice) that impose more stringent conditions on data transfers and suggest that local processing is preferable to ensure compliance with security and privacy standards. These requirements do not constitute a blanket local storage mandate but make local storage a practical solution for ensuring compliance with security obligations, especially for sensitive data.
Notes: BGK Timeframe: Since November 2013, last amended in 2024

Law Name: Services Tax Act (Act 807) 2018
Mapping Rationale:
Section 24 of the Service Tax Act 2018 (Act 807) sets out the obligations for recordkeeping by taxable persons. Every taxable person must keep complete, accurate, and up-to-date records of all transactions that affect or may affect their liability to service tax. This includes records of all taxable services provided or received (such as invoices, receipts, debit and credit notes), records of imported taxable services, and any other records as may be determined by the Director General. These records must be preserved for seven years from the most recent date to which they relate, must be kept in either the national language or English, and must be retained in Malaysia unless otherwise approved by the Director General under specific conditions.

If records are maintained in an electronically readable format, they must be stored in a way that allows for ready access and conversion into writing. If records originally kept in manual form are later converted to electronic form, the original manual versions must also be preserved. Copies of records are admissible in legal proceedings to the same extent as the originals. This section also applies to any person, other than a taxable person, who acquires imported taxable services in the course of business. Failure to comply with any of these requirements is an offence and may result in a fine of up to RM50,000, imprisonment of up to three years, or both. However, these obligations do not apply to foreign registered persons.

Note that this requirement was available under the repealed Goods and Services Tax Act 2014.

Law Name: Income Tax Act (Act 53) 1967
Mapping Rationale:
Section 82 imposes a legal duty on all businesses to maintain proper records and, where applicable, issue receipts. Every business must keep accurate and sufficient records for at least seven years from the end of the relevant income year to allow tax authorities to determine taxable income or losses. If gross takings exceed RM150,000 from goods or RM100,000 from services, the business must issue serially numbered printed receipts for each transaction and keep duplicates. Businesses that file late returns must also keep records for seven years from the filing date.

If a sales recording machine is used, the receipt requirement may be waived, but only if the machine records all transactions accurately. The Director General may set or waive requirements for recordkeeping and receipts and may also request audited financial statements under the Companies Act 2016 if existing records are inadequate. Entries must be made within 60 days of each transaction. Records kept electronically must be readable, accessible, and convertible to written form; if manual records are later digitized, the originals must be preserved.

Moreover, All records that relate to any business in Malaysia shall be kept and retained in Malaysia. Law Name: Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010
Mapping Rationale:
Malaysia has a comprehensive data protection framework established through the Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010, which applies to the processing of personal data in commercial transactions. The PDPA regulates how personal data can be collected, used, and disclosed, and it imposes obligations on data users (companies and organizations) to protect the personal data of individuals.

Moreover, the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Bill 2024 (Act A1727) amendments to the PDPA further enhance this framework by introducing mandatory data breach notifications, extending data processor obligations, and increasing penalties for non-compliance, aligning Malaysia’s privacy regulations more closely with international standards like the EU’s GDPR. Specifically, data Breach Notification (Section 12b) requires data controllers (including those in banking and communications sectors) to notify the Personal Data Protection Commissioner and affected data subjects in the event of a data breach, especially if the breach poses significant harm. Moreover, penalties (Amendment of Section 5) prescribes that the penalties for non-compliance with the Security Principle or data breach requirements have been increased to 1 million ringgit or imprisonment of up to three years, or both.

In addition to the PDPA, sector-specific codes of practice also exist for industries like banking, finance, and communications, but these operate within the comprehensive legal framework provided by the PDPA.
Notes:

Law Name: Computer Crimes Act (Act 563) 1997
Mapping Rationale:
Malaysia previous cybersecurity law was based on Computer Crimes Act (Act 563) 1997, it criminalizes various cybercrimes, such as unauthorized access to computers, modification of computer content, and other malicious cyber activities. However, it mainly addresses cyber offenses rather than a broader cybersecurity framework. The Cyber Security Act 2024 now provides a comprehensive framework to address national cybersecurity threats and regulate service providers.

The new Cyber Security Act (Act 854) 2024 enhances Malaysia’s national cybersecurity efforts by:
	1. Establishing a National Cyber Security Committee, responsible for overseeing cybersecurity policies and national coordination (Part III - Duties and Powers of Chief Executive).
	2. Defining roles for critical information infrastructure entities and mandating them to comply with cybersecurity risk assessments, audits, and notifications of cybersecurity incidents. Sections 15-24 cover the responsibilities and duties of entities designated as national critical information infrastructure.
	3. Regulating cybersecurity service providers through a licensing regime to ensure that those offering services like managed security operation center monitoring and penetration testing adhere to national standards. Sections 27-34 focus on the licensing of cybersecurity service providers.
	4. Strengthening enforcement through powers of investigation, search, and seizure, allowing the government to respond effectively to cybersecurity threats (Sections 36-52), thus, enabling the enforcement of cybersecurity regulations and the management of cyber incidents.
This new law positions Malaysia to better handle cyber risks and threats to its critical infrastructures.

Section 24 of the Service Tax Act 2018 (Act 807) sets out the obligations for recordkeeping by taxable persons. Every taxable person must keep complete, accurate, and up-to-date records of all transactions that affect or may affect their liability to service tax. This includes records of all taxable services provided or received (such as invoices, receipts, debit and credit notes), records of imported taxable services, and any other records as may be determined by the Director General. If records are maintained in an electronically readable format, they must be stored in a way that allows for ready access and conversion into writing. This section also applies to any person, other than a taxable person, who acquires imported taxable services in the course of business. Failure to comply with any of these requirements is an offence and may result in a fine of up to RM50,000, imprisonment of up to three years, or both. Law Name: Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010
Mapping Rationale:
The Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Bill 2024 (Act A1727) amendments to the Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010 (PDPA) introduced new requirements, including the appointment of Data Protection Officers (DPOs) and the implementation of Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), marking significant changes compared to the original PDPA 2010. Section 12a (1) of the 2024 PDPA amendment mandates that a data controller must appoint one or more Data Protection Officers (DPOs). The DPO is accountable for ensuring compliance with the PDPA, which applies horizontally across all sectors. This is a significant change from the 2010 version, where no explicit requirement for a DPO was mandated.

The 2024 amendments also introduced a requirement for DPIAs in specific cases where data processing activities pose a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. This is especially relevant for large-scale processing of sensitive personal data or new technologies. Similar to the DPO requirement, the DPIA requirement applies horizontally across all sectors when high-risk processing is involved. Another significant change from the 2010 PDPA, as organizations are now required to assess and mitigate risks through formal DPIA procedures.
Notes:

Mapping Rationale:
From the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Bill 2024 (Act A1727) amendments, there is no explicit provision that allows the government to access personal data without a court order.

The Personal Data Protection Act (Act 709) 2010 PDPA Section 45(2)(a)(i) exempts personal data from the consent requirement if it is processed for the prevention or detection of crime, or for the purposes of investigations. And Section 121 grants authorized officers the power to request the production of documents or data (including computerized data) to ensure compliance with the PDPA. An authorized officer shall have the powers of a police officer of whatever rank as provided for under the Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593)  in relation to investigation, and such powers shall be in addition to and not in derogation of, the powers provided for under this Act (Section 112 Power of investigation). A Magistrate may issue a warrant for an officer to search premises and seize evidence related to an offense, with or without assistance and by force if needed (Section 113 Search and seizure with warrant). However, where delay could harm the investigation, an officer may search without a warrant using the same powers (Section 114 Search and seizure without warrant).

These specific sectoral guidelines indicate that while court orders are generally required for accessing personal data, exceptions exist, particularly for criminal investigations and regulatory functions, where data can be accessed without consent or court intervention.

Law Name: Personal Data Protection Act 2012
Mapping Rationale:
According to Section 26, an organisation may only transfer personal data outside Singapore if it has taken appropriate steps to ensure that:
- it will comply with the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) obligations in respect of the transferred personal data while it remains in its possession or under its control; and
- the recipient outside of Singapore is bound by legally enforceable obligations to provide a standard of protection to the personal data transferred that is comparable to that under the PDPA.

Law Name: Personal Data Protection Act 2012
Mapping Rationale:
The Personal Data Protection Act 2012 (PDPA) provides a baseline standard of protection for personal data in Singapore. It complements sector-specific legislative and regulatory frameworks such as the Banking Act and Insurance Act, Healthcare Services Act, Telecommunications Act, etc. The PDPA comprises various requirements governing the collection, use, disclosure and care of personal data in Singapore. Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) administers and enforces the PDPA.

Moreover, the PDPA amendment in 2021 introduces a number of key reforms, including mandatory data breach notification requirements, amendments to the consent obligation, offences for egregious mishandling of personal data, prohibitions relating to the use of dictionary attacks and address-harvesting software, and the PDPC's power to accept voluntary undertakings as part of its enforcement regime.
Notes:
BGK Timeframe: Since 2012 last amended on 1 February 2021 | BGK Note: "The PDPA does not expressly include cookies in its definition of personal data. However, cookies can qualify as personal data if they fall within the broad definition of personal data, that is, if they identify an individual either by themselves or together with other information, which the organisation has or is likely to have access to. Likewise, digital fingerprinting and online behavioural advertising technologies will fall under the ambit of the PDPA insofar as they deal with personal data. The PDPC of Singapore has issued guidance that expressly discusses cookies as a way in which personal data is collected, used or disclosed. In essence, the Commission recognises that many internet activities today are dependent on the use of cookies and that unnecessarily restricting the use of cookies will impede the use of the internet. However, because cookies can potentially collect personal data, organisations must be mindful of using them for individuals' online activities. If cookies containing personal data arise from individuals who voluntarily provide it, their consent can be deemed to be provided for the purpose for which the personal data was provided. However, the obligation to obtain an individual's consent to collect personal data rests with the organisation that is collecting it, whether itself or through data intermediaries. Where an organisation operates a website that a third party uses to collect personal data, and the website operator itself is not collecting this personal data, the obligation is on the third party organisation to obtain the required consent."

Law Name: Cybersecurity Act 2018
Mapping Rationale: Cybersecurity Act 2018 establishes a legal framework for the oversight and maintenance of national cybersecurity in Singapore. The key objectives of the Cybersecurity Act are to: (i) strengthen the protection of Critical Information Infrastructure against cyber-attacks; (ii) authorize the government to prevent and respond to cybersecurity threats and incidents; (iii); establish a framework for sharing cybersecurity information, and (iv) establish a licensing framework for cybersecurity service providers. Amendments to the Act were made in May 2024 to update the Act so that it keeps pace with the developments in the cyber threat landscape, as well as our evolving technological operating context. The key amendments: (i) updated existing provisions relating to cybersecurity of Critical Information Infrastructure, and (ii) expanded CSA’s oversight to cover new classes of regulated entities.
Notes: BGK Timeframe: Since 2018 | BGK Note: ‘Cybersecurity Act 2018 mandates the identification and designation of CIIs—computer systems essential for delivering vital services. Owners of CIIs are required to implement robust cybersecurity measures and comply with codes of practice to prevent and respond to cyber threats. CII owners must promptly report cybersecurity incidents to the Commissioner of Cybersecurity. The Act grants the Commissioner authority to investigate and manage such incidents to mitigate potential impacts. Cybersecurity Act 2018 introduces a licensing framework for providers of specific cybersecurity services, ensuring that these services meet established standards and are delivered by qualified professionals. It also formalizes the CSA's role as the national authority overseeing cybersecurity, responsible for implementing policies, coordinating responses to cyber incidents, and promoting cybersecurity awareness.’ This write-up has been re-written by Singapore feedback.

Law Name: Personal Data Protection Act 2012
Mapping Rationale: Section 25 of the PDPA requires an organisation to cease retaining its documents containing personal data, or remove the means by which the personal data can be associated with particular individuals, as soon as it is reasonable to assume that the purpose for which that personal data was collected is no longer being served by retention of the personal data, and retention is no longer necessary for legal or business purposes. This obligation to cease the retention of personal data is referred to in these Guidelines as the Retention Limitation Obligation.
Notes:
BGK Timeframe: Since 2012 last amended on 1 February 2021 | BGK Note: In practice, the retention period for personal data under the PDPA will depend on the following factors: a) The purpose(s) for which the personal data was collected. That is: i. personal data may be retained so long as one or more of the purposes for which it was collected remains valid; and ii. personal data must not be kept by an organisation “just in case” it may be needed for other purposes that have not been notified to the individual concerned. b) Other legal or business purposes for which retention of the personal data by the organisation is necessary. For example, this may include situations where: i. the personal data is required for an ongoing legal action involving the organisation; ii. retention of the personal data is necessary in order to comply with the organisation’s obligations under other applicable laws, regulations, international/regional/bilateral standards which require the retention of personal data; or iii. the personal data is required for an organisation to carry out its business operations, such as to generate annual reports, or performance forecasts.
An organisation should review the personal data it holds on a regular basis to determine if that personal data is still needed. An organisation which holds a large quantity of different types of personal data may have to implement varying retention periods for each type of personal data as appropriate.

Mapping Rationale:
In addition to comprehensive legislation that applies horizontally across all sectors, China has also developed and implemented a wide range of sector-specific regulations related to data protection, offering detailed guidance tailored to different industries. For example, in just the first half of 2024 alone, the Chinese government issued over 20 national laws, industry regulations, and local policies concerning data security. A selection of these is listed below.

Education sector:
The General Office of the Ministry of Education Issued the “Management Standards for the Entry and Removal of Digital Educational Resources on the National Smart Education Platform”. According to the Standards, platform service providers must comply with relevant laws, regulations, and national standards, and adopt technical and other necessary measures to ensure the security of the platform and its resources, as well as retain network logs in accordance with the law.

Energy sector:

It emphasizes the implementation of data security laws and regulations, enhanced oversight of data circulation, and the creation of a secure and reliable environment for data exchange. Law Name: Reserve Bank of India Directive 2018
Mapping Rationale:
In April 2018, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued a one-page directive  vide circular DPSS.CO.OD.No 2785/06.08.005/2017-18  stating that, within six months, all payment data held by payment companies should be held in local facilities. The Directive noted that this would help the RBI gain "unfettered supervisory access" to transaction data, which it needs to ensure proper monitoring.

Following a negative response from international payment companies such as MasterCard, Visa and American Express, the RBI has proposed (in "Frequently Asked Questions" of its website) to ease this restriction, so as to allow payment firms to store data offshore, as long as a copy was kept in India. The RBI has further clarified that for cross border transaction data consisting of a foreign component and domestic component, a copy of the domestic component may be stored abroad, if required.

With respect to processing of payment transactions outside India, the RBI requires that the data must be stored only in India after processing and should be deleted from systems abroad and brought back to India no later than 24 hours after processing. Any subsequent activity such as settlement processing after payment processing done outside India, this must be undertaken on a real time basis pursuant to which the data must be stored only in India.

The RBI has clarified that banks, especially foreign banks, can continue to store banking data abroad but in respect of domestic payment transactions, the data must be stored only in India.
Notes:
BGK Timeframe: Since April 2018 | BGK Note: The legal part written herein is accurate. In April 2018, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued a, mandating all payment system providers to ensure that the entire data related to payment systems operated by them are stored in a system only in India. The Directive noted that this would help the RBI gain "unfettered supervisory access" to transaction data, which would ensure better monitoring.

RBI has clarified that for cross-border transaction data, consisting of a foreign component and a domestic component, a copy of the domestic component may be stored abroad if required. Further it was clarified that there is no bar on processing payment transactions outside India if so desired by the PSOs. However, the data shall be stored only in India after the processing. The complete end-to-end transaction details should be part of the data.

With respect to the processing of payment transactions outside India, the RBI requires that the data must be stored only in India after processing and should be deleted from systems abroad and brought back to India no later than one business day or 24 hours from payment processing, whichever is earlier. Any subsequent activity, such as settlement processing after payment processing done outside India, must be undertaken on a real-time basis, pursuant to which the data must be stored only in India.

The RBI has clarified that in case of banks, especially foreign banks, earlier specifically permitted to store the banking data abroad, they may continue to do so; however, in respect of domestic payment transactions, the data shall be stored only in India.

The directive is issued under Section 10(2) read with Section 18 of Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007

Law Name: Information Technology (Reasonable Security Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules 2011
Mapping Rationale:
Rule 6 of the Information Technology Rules 2011 provides that cross-border data transfers of sensitive personal data or information can be made to any other corporate entity or person in India or to any other country that ensures the same level of data protection as provided under the Rules. Disclosure of sensitive personal data or information by a corporation to any third party shall require prior permission from the provider of such information, who has provided such information under lawful contract or otherwise, unless such disclosure has been agreed to in the contract between the body corporate and provider of information, or where the disclosure is necessary for compliance of a legal obligation. Sensitive personal information includes passwords, financial information such as bank account or credit/debit card details, sexual orientation, physical, mental health condition, biometric information etc.

According to the Clarification on Information Technology Rules, published in August 2011, corporations providing services relating to collection, storage, dealing or handling of sensitive personal data or information under contractual obligation with any legal entity located within or outside India are not subject to the requirement of Rule 6.

Mapping Rationale:
As per the SEBI Listing Regulations, a listed entity (i.e. an entity which is listed on the stock market) is required to have a policy for the preservation of documents. The SEBI Listing Regulations require that records, books, papers and documents of the company be preserved as per the following classifications:
i) Schedule I - to be preserved permanently. Documents listed under these schedule include incorporation documents, share certificates, register of minutes of board meetings, register of members etc.
ii) Schedule II – to be preserved for eight years. Documents listed under this schedule include books of accounts, attendance register of board meetings, register of debenture holders etc.
iii) Schedule III – to be preserved for a minimum period of five years or such higher period as may be determine by the board of directors of the company. Documents listed under this schedule include register of stock options, register of directors and key managerial personnel, disclosures made under applicable company laws etc.

Law Name: Information Technology Act No.21 2000
Mapping Rationale:
Section 69 (Power to issue directions for interception or monitoring or decryption of any information through
any computer resource) of the Information Technology Act 2000, as amended by the Information Technology (Amendment) Act 2008, gives the central and state governments the power to direct any agency to intercept, monitor or decrypt, or cause to be intercepted, monitored or decrypted any information transmitted, received or stored through any computer resources. The government must be satisfied that this is necessary in the interest of the sovereignty, security or defense of India. The government may require any subscriber or intermediary or any person in charge of the computer resource to extend all facilities and technical assistance necessary to decrypt the information.

(Note: Section 69A provides power to issue directions for blocking for public access of any information through any
computer resource, and Section 69B provides power to authorise to monitor and collect traffic data or information through any computer
resource for cyber security).
Notes: BGK Timeframe: Since December 2000, last amended in 2008

Law Name: Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Interception, Monitoring and Decryption of Information) Rules 2009
Mapping Rationale: The Rules provide that the officer so designated by the Central Government under the Rules (known as 'Designated Officer') can on the receipt of request from any nodal officer of a government organisation or a competent court or by an order of any agency of the government can block access by the public to any information transmitted, received, stored or hosted in any computer resource. The request will be examined by a committee consisting of the designated officer and its chairperson and representatives, who shall determine if the information must be blocked.
Notes: BGK Timeframe: Since 2009

On the occurrence of any public emergency or in the interest of public safety, the Central Government or a State Government or any officer specially authorised in this behalf by the Central Government or a State Government, may, if satisfied that it is necessary or expedient so to do, in the interest of the sovereignty and integrity of India, defence and security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, or for preventing incitement to the commission of any offence, subject to such procedure and safeguards as may be prescribed, and for reasons to be recorded in writing, by order—

The Digital Personal Data Protection Bill, 2023 under special provisions in Chapter IV Article 17 (2) (a) gives the government powers to exempt state agencies from the law: by such instrumentality of the State as the Central Government may notify, in the interests of sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, maintenance of public order or preventing incitement to any cognizable offence relating to any of these, and the processing by the Central Government of any personal data that such instrumentality may furnish to it.

Law Name: Law on Personal Data Protection
Mapping Rationale: Law on Protection of Personal Information does not mandate infrastructure requirement. Moreover, following Article 18.6 of the Law on Transparency of Public Information, enacted by the Parliament in 2021, it is mandatory for the data controller's system to fully adhere to the government's communication and information technology guidelines and security standards. There is no requirement for the location of the information processing server.
Notes:
BGK Timeframe: Since December 2021 | BGK Note: Under Article 20 of the Law on Protection of Personal Information approved by the State Parliament in 2021, Data Controller must: 1. Establish internal procedures to safeguard the security of individuals' data and apply these procedures in their operations. 2. Outline measures to be taken for data loss, including plans to inform the data owner and relevant government agencies as per the law. 3. Commit to taking all necessary measures to ensure the integrity, confidentiality, and accessibility of the information system for collecting, processing, and using data. 4. Implement procedures and guidelines to restrict the use, deletion, and anonymization of information to ensure the security of data processing operations.

As per Article 6.2 of the Law on Transparency of Public Information passed by the Parliament in 2021, the data controller must gather, process, utilize, manage, arrange, and guarantee the security of the information. It must also take other necessary measures within the scope of its functions as specified in the law. According to Article 18.6 of the law, the data controller's system must adhere to the government's communication and information technology guidelines and security standards. There is no requirement for the location of the information processing server.

Law Name: Law on Personal Data Protection
Mapping Rationale:
Mongolia does not mandate DPO or DPIA requirement.

Article 22.1 of the Law on the Protection of Personal Information explicitly requires the data processor to immediately report any breach during data collection and processing to the data controller. As stipulated in Article 22.2, should the breach impact the rights and legal interests of the data owner, the data controller must promptly notify the data owner. Article 4.1.3 of the law defines "promptly" within a short, reasonable period. The data owner is empowered, following Article 22.4, to file a complaint with the relevant authorities if they believe their rights and legal interests have been violated, as elaborated in Article 22.2 of this law. Moreover, the data controller and data processor shall conduct a risk assessment to ensure the security of data processing operations (Article 20.1.5).
Notes: BGK Timeframe: Since December 2021 | BGK Note: Article 20.1 is a general security risk assessment obligation, which may include DPIA-like activities, especially for high-risk processing, but it is not a full DPIA requirement unless clarified elsewhere in the law.
